transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Ava Brooks (Zenora Product), Marcus Li (Zenora Eng), Janelle Ortiz (Zenora Security)

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm lena from redwood, and ravi and i will run through a quick hosted api demo — chat and text generation basics, focused on streaming, params and retries.
[00:12] Ava: thanks lena, excited. we want to see latency and cost tradeoffs, and a bit on security.
[00:18] Ravi: great — quick agenda, we'll do a short intro, a live demo calling the hosted api, show streaming, parameter tuning (temp/top_p/max_tokens), then retries/idempotency and some cost/latency notes. any must-ask things up front?
[00:30] Marcus: timeline: we need a pilot asap, ideally next week; latency target for inference is around 150 to 200 milliseconds p95 for short chat prompts.
[00:38] Janelle: and security — we need to know about encryption at rest, KMS options, and audit logs — SOC2 is a must.
[00:45] Lena: noted. quick intro to product — redwood hosted api gives text generation, chat, embeddings; we expose streaming and chunked responses, configurable params and built-in retry policies. we also have a model catalog with pre-profiled performance.
[01:05] Ravi: i'm going to share my screen and run a small demo. (screen share starts)
[01:18] Ravi: here is a curl example we often show — simple chat call: POST /v1/chat/completions, body contains messages, model id, and params. i'll switch to node snippet to show streaming via server-sent events.
[01:35] Ravi: code: const resp = await client.chat.completions.create({ model: "redwood-large-v2", messages, stream: true, temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, max_tokens: 256 });
[01:52] Ava: quick q — what's the default retry behavior if we get a 5xx or rate limit?
[01:58] Ravi: by default we return a 429 or 5xx back to you, our SDKs implement exponential backoff retries for idempotent requests. we recommend client-side retry with jitter; server side we do automatic transient retries for internal infra but not for user requests that may be non-idempotent. we also expose idempotency keys for longer-running ops; use an x-idempotency-key header.
[02:25] Marcus: and how do you handle duplicate streaming events if a retry triggers?
[02:30] Ravi: good question — streaming sessions are terminated on error and if client retries with same idempotency key we'll resume a fresh deterministic response where possible; some models are non-deterministic so exact byte-for-byte resume isn't guaranteed. usually we recommend checkpointing by prompt id.
[02:50] (short pause, typing)
[03:12] Ravi: demo continues — i'm toggling stream: you should see tokens appear as SSE chunks; this is useful for chat UX to show progressive replies and reduces perceived latency.
[03:28] (demo shows streaming tokens, small stutters)
[03:45] Ava: looks nice — what's the average per-token latency when streaming vs full response?
[03:52] Ravi: streaming reduces time-to-first-byte — for short responses we typically hit first token in ~30-80ms depending on region and model, full response time will include compute for whole output. for your sub-200ms p95 target for short prompts we recommend a smaller tuned model or request-level batching disabled, plus prefix caching.
[04:18] Janelle: prefix caching — can you say more? data residency concerns too — we can't send certain PII off-region.
[04:25] Lena: prefix (KV) caching stores common prefixes and kv-cache between requests to reduce per-token compute. for data residency we have region pinning on hosted and private control plane options for full on-prem. for pilot we can pin to eu-west or us-east depending on your data policy.
[04:48] Marcus: what's the cost profile — tokens per request cost and effective throughput?
[04:54] Ravi: cost depends on model size and quantization, we provide per-token pricing in the proposal but ballpark: smaller LLMs could be X/1M tokens and larger Y/1M tokens. Optimize (the tooling) suggests batching/caching and quantization settings to cut unit cost. we'll send a pricing sheet after.
[05:15] Ava: any builtin rate limits and how to handle bursts?
[05:20] Lena: hosted API has per-account quotas and per-route rate limits; for bursts you can request increased quotas. Dedicated offers predictable throughput with reserved GPU pools. You can also configure graceful degradation policies — route to cheaper model variant on high load.
[05:39] Marcus: can we see an example of parameter tuning — e.g., temperature and top_p?
[05:44] Ravi: sure — i'll change temperature to 0.0 for deterministic answers and to 0.8 for creative. top_p at 0.9 keeps nucleus sampling. i'll show how outputs differ in real time.
[06:05] (demo shows difference in responses, some transcription noise)
[06:40] Ava: about retries — do you expose retry headers or request ids to correlate logs?
[06:46] Ravi: yes we return x-request-id and x-region headers; our SDKs log these automatically. we'll share a sample log format. request ids let you correlate with our support and engineer team.
[07:02] Janelle: security questions — encryption at rest, KMS, SSO.
[07:08] Lena: hosted supports customer-managed keys via KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK in some regions) for Private we support HSM options. we store audit logs and provide retention controls, SOC2 compliance is in place; we'll share our security pack. for SSO we support SAML/Okta provisioning and RBAC in the console.
[07:33] Janelle: do logs contain raw prompts? we need controls to redact PII from request logs.
[07:39] Ravi: you can opt out of retaining prompts in logs; we also offer on-the-fly redaction via our SDK or proxy layer and we can work with your team on PII suppression. for the pilot we recommend submitting a reduced sample set.
[07:58] Marcus: latency vs cost question again — is there an easy knob to trade them?
[08:03] Ravi: yes — choose smaller models, enable quantized variants, turn off batching for low-latency single user flows, enable prefix caching for repeat prompts. Optimize gives recommendations based on traced workloads.
[08:18] Ava: show us the console briefly?
[08:22] Ravi: switching tabs — console shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-model dashboards, tracing and per-route analytics. here's the rollout UI for canarying a model to 10% traffic.
[08:40] (clicks through console, opens tracing)
[08:52] Lena: we also have built-in evals — you can tie prompt sets to regression alerts so quality drops trigger notifications.
[08:59] Ava: good — we're worried about hallucinations in finance answers. can you limit or enforce structured output?
[09:06] Ravi: yes — use function/tool-calling or structured output templates and validate server-side. also you can set max_tokens and stop sequences to reduce runaways. and use temperature 0 and top_p low for deterministic outputs in business logic.
[09:27] Marcus: what about SDKs and language support?
[09:30] Ravi: official SDKs for Python, Node, and a thin curl example. we also have Postman collections and example microservices.
[09:40] (small cross-talk)
[10:05] Lena: i want to cover retries in a bit more depth — common pattern we recommend: exponential backoff with full jitter, cap at 3 retries for transient 5xx/429, and use idempotency keys for anything that mutates state. also include circuit-breaker logic to avoid cascading failures.
[10:25] Marcus: do you provide guidance for rate-limit headers?
[10:28] Ravi: yes — rate-limit headers indicate remaining and reset; SDKs surface this. we'll share a sample snippet in the benchmark doc.
[10:40] Ava: can we run a 1-week pilot with a small traffic set and benchmarks?
[10:44] Lena: absolutely — typical pilot includes a 1-week performance benchmark with your sample prompts (we'll test 1k to 10k queries/day depending on your volume), measure p50/p95 latency, token costs, and quality metrics. 
[11:00] (typing, notes)
[11:20] Ravi: for the pilot we'll recommend three model variants: a low-latency small model, a mid-tier balanced model, and a high-quality large model. we'll run the same prompt set against each and provide cost/latency QPS tradeoffs.
[11:40] Janelle: for compliance we'd need the pilot to run in eu-west-1 and no logs retained by default — possible?
[11:46] Lena: yes we can pin region and turn off prompt retention. we'll note that in the scope doc.
[12:00] (short silence)
[12:15] Ava: any red flags or known limitations?
[12:18] Ravi: small items: streaming can increase connection churn if clients don't handle SSE well; retries can lead to duplicated tokens if idempotency isn't used; very low-latency targets may require deployment to Dedicated or Private with reserved capacity.
[12:40] Marcus: analytics and billing — do you provide per-route cost at token level?
[12:45] Lena: yes, console shows token-level cost by model and route, and we offer fine-grained tags for cost allocation.
[13:00] Ava: ok let's recap next steps.
[13:05] Lena: recap — we'll send pilot scope and pricing, ravi will share benchmark spreadsheet and sample logs, customer will provide prompt sample and PII redaction list, security will review SOC2/KMS Qs and we'll schedule a security deep-dive mid-next week.
[13:25] Marcus: sounds good. i'll get sample prompts to you by friday.
[13:29] Janelle: i'll compile security questions and send ahead of the deep-dive.
[13:33] Lena: perfect, we'll follow up with a calendar invite for kickoff. thanks everyone.
[13:40] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "dedicate" instead of "dedicated"), speaker overlaps labeled simply with names, some punctuation missing as in real transcriptions. Shared artifacts: pilot scope doc (link: https://redwood.app/proposals/zenora-pilot), benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/zenora-2026), security pack (link: https://redwood.app/security/redwood-security-pack.pdf).
notes: Customer interested in 1-week pilot, regional pinning, KMS and SOC2. AE/SE to provide pricing and benchmark artifacts. Security deep-dive to be scheduled.
